nodes.title: Types of Number, Factors and Multiples

prerequisites.statement: Recall multiplication facts (times tables) up to 12 × 12 and divide one whole number by another with no remainder.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every factor tree, every list of factors and every prime-factorisation in this lesson is just repeated division by a small prime; without fast recall of multiplication facts, finding even one factor tree becomes a long trial-and-error search.

prerequisites.statement: Write a fraction with a numerator and a denominator, and recognise that a fraction $\dfrac ab$ represents a division $a\div b$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Rational numbers are defined as fractions of integers, and finding a reciprocal means flipping numerator and denominator; without this, both ideas are just memorised rules with no meaning.

prerequisites.statement: Read and write the place value of digits in a whole number (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, and beyond).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Converting numbers between words and figures, and using zero as a place holder, both depend directly on place value.

prerequisites.statement: Understand that integers include negative whole numbers as well as positive whole numbers and zero.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The set of integers $\mathbb Z$ sits between the natural numbers and the rational numbers in this lesson's number-families diagram, and confusing integers with natural numbers (no negatives) makes the whole diagram meaningless.

prerequisites.statement: Recall multiplication facts (times tables) up to 12 × 12.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A square or a cube is nothing more than a short multiplication repeated two or three times; without instant recall of multiplication facts, evaluating even $7^2$ becomes slow, error-prone counting.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise a square number and a cube number from Lesson 1 (e.g. that 36 and 125 are a square and a cube respectively).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson builds the square/cube idea into an operation (raising to a power) and its reverse (taking a root); a student who cannot yet recognise a square number will not see why the square root of a perfect square is always exact.

prerequisites.statement: Know that a fraction $\dfrac ab$ represents the division $a\div b$, and that a terminating decimal has a fixed number of digits after the point.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding the square root of a fraction or a decimal (e.g. $\sqrt{0.09}$ or $\sqrt{\tfrac{25}{64}}$) depends on being able to move freely between the fraction and decimal forms of the same number.

prerequisites.statement: Understand that integers include negative whole numbers, and know the basic rule that multiplying two negative numbers gives a positive result.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Deciding whether $(-4)^3$ and $(-4)^2$ are positive or negative, and whether a negative number has a real square root, both depend on this rule.

prerequisites.statement: Add, subtract, multiply and divide positive whole numbers fluently.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every rule in this lesson for directed numbers and decimals builds on top of the same basic arithmetic facts; a shaky multiplication fact makes a correct sign-rule application still come out numerically wrong.

prerequisites.statement: Understand that integers include negative whole numbers as well as positive whole numbers and zero (from Lesson 1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Ordering numbers and combining them with directed-number rules both require already accepting negative numbers as genuine numbers with a position on the number line, not merely 'positive numbers with a minus sign attached'.

prerequisites.statement: Recall squares and cubes, and evaluate a square or cube root (from Lesson 2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The 'Indices' step of BIDMAS requires evaluating powers and roots correctly before combining them with the rest of an expression; a slip here corrupts every later step even if the order of operations itself is applied perfectly.

prerequisites.statement: Read and compare the place value of digits in a decimal number.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Lining up decimal points to add or subtract, and comparing two decimals of different lengths (e.g. $-0.6$ against $-0.06$), both depend on correctly reading which digit sits in which place.

prerequisites.statement: Find the HCF of two numbers, using prime factorisation if needed (from Lesson 1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Simplifying a fraction to its lowest terms is exactly dividing both numerator and denominator by their HCF; without this, simplifying relies on guesswork rather than a reliable method.

prerequisites.statement: Find the LCM of two numbers (from Lesson 1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Adding or subtracting fractions with different denominators requires rewriting them over a common denominator, and the LCM of the two denominators gives the smallest, most manageable common denominator to use.

prerequisites.statement: Find the reciprocal of a fraction or an integer (from Lesson 1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Dividing by a fraction is defined as multiplying by its reciprocal; without a secure grip on what a reciprocal is, the division rule becomes a meaningless 'flip the second one' instruction.

prerequisites.statement: Read the place value of digits after a decimal point.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Converting a decimal to a fraction (e.g. $0.35=\tfrac{35}{100}$) depends on correctly reading which place value each decimal digit occupies.

prerequisites.statement: Understand that $a^n$ means $a$ multiplied by itself $n$ times (repeated multiplication).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every law of indices in this lesson (the addition law, the subtraction law, the power-of-a-power law) is derived by counting copies of the base being multiplied together; without this starting picture, the laws are just rules to memorise rather than facts that follow logically.

prerequisites.statement: Find the square root and cube root of simple perfect squares and perfect cubes (e.g. $\sqrt{81}=9$, $\sqrt[3]{27}=3$) (from Lesson 2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Fractional indices are defined directly in terms of roots ($a^{1/n}=\sqrt[n]a$), so evaluating $81^{1/2}$ or $27^{1/3}$ by hand depends entirely on already knowing these root values.

prerequisites.statement: Find the reciprocal of a fraction or integer, and simplify a fraction (from Lesson 4).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A negative index is defined as a reciprocal ($a^{-n}=\tfrac1{a^n}$), so evaluating any negative-index expression depends on being comfortable finding and simplifying reciprocals.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise small numbers as powers of a common base (e.g. $4=2^2$, $8=2^3$, $9=3^2$, $16=2^4$, $27=3^3$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Solving an index equation like $3^x=\tfrac1{27}$ or writing $4^3\times2^{-2}$ as a single power of $2$ depends on first spotting that every number involved can be rewritten as a power of the SAME base.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by powers of $10$, by moving the decimal point.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Converting a number into or out of standard form IS exactly this skill, applied in a specific direction: moving the decimal point and tracking how many places it moved.

prerequisites.statement: Apply the multiplication and division laws of indices, $a^m\times a^n=a^{m+n}$ and $a^m\div a^n=a^{m-n}$ (from Lesson 5).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Multiplying or dividing two numbers in standard form means combining their powers of ten using exactly these laws on the index $n$; without them, the power-of-ten part of a calculation has no reliable method.

prerequisites.statement: Round a number to a given number of significant figures.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Standard-form answers in context (e.g. a calculated distance or a population density) are usually required to a stated number of significant figures, most often 3, and $A$ itself must be rounded correctly before the final answer is written down.

prerequisites.statement: Evaluate zero and negative integer indices (from Lesson 5).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Small numbers in standard form always use a NEGATIVE power of ten, and correctly reading what a negative index means (reciprocal, not a negative value) prevents the number itself from being mistaken for something negative.

prerequisites.statement: Identify the place value of any digit in a whole number or decimal (units, tens, hundreds, tenths, hundredths, \ldots).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Rounding depends entirely on correctly locating the rounding digit (the last digit kept) and the decider (the digit immediately after it), both of which are identified purely by place value.

prerequisites.statement: Perform simple mental arithmetic with small whole numbers and one-digit decimals (adding, multiplying, dividing).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Estimating is only useful if the rounded calculation can genuinely be done in your head; without fluent mental arithmetic on small numbers, the whole point of rounding to $1$ significant figure first is lost.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise perfect squares and their square roots up to at least $12^2=144$ (from Lesson 2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A useful estimating trick replaces an awkward root with the root of a nearby perfect square (e.g. $\sqrt{48}\approx\sqrt{49}=7$), which only works if the perfect squares themselves are already known by heart.

prerequisites.statement: Compare the size of two decimals (from Lesson 4).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Judging whether an estimate is an over-estimate or an under-estimate means comparing the (simplified) rounded calculation against the exact value, which is a direct application of comparing two decimal numbers.

prerequisites.statement: Round a number to a given place value, number of decimal places, or number of significant figures (from Lesson 7).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The rounding UNIT (the size of the interval a bound is built from) is identified directly from how the original value was rounded, so bounds cannot be found without first correctly identifying that rounding accuracy.

prerequisites.statement: Read and write the inequality symbols $\leqslant$ and $<$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: An error interval is written as a mixed inequality (e.g. $6.5\leqslant l<7.5$), with a DIFFERENT symbol at each end, so the meaning of each symbol must already be secure before this notation can be used correctly.

prerequisites.statement: Apply the four operations ($+,-,\times,\div$) to decimals confidently (from Lessons 4 and 7).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding the bounds of a calculation means carrying out the SAME arithmetic operation twice (once for the upper bound, once for the lower), so fluent decimal arithmetic is needed to avoid the bounds method itself being obscured by calculation slips.

prerequisites.statement: Explain why dividing by a smaller number gives a larger result, and dividing by a larger number gives a smaller result (from Lesson 7's estimation work).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Deciding WHICH bound of each quantity to use for the upper or lower bound of a quotient depends entirely on this same size relationship already met when predicting over- and under-estimates.

prerequisites.statement: Find the HCF of two or more numbers, using prime factorisation if needed (from Lesson 1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Simplifying a ratio to its lowest terms is exactly dividing every term by their HCF; without this, a ratio can be left only partially simplified.

prerequisites.statement: Convert between units of the same quantity (e.g. kg to g, km to cm).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A ratio can only be simplified once both quantities are measured in the SAME unit; a ratio like $2\text{ kg}:500\text{ g}$ is meaningless to simplify directly until converted.

prerequisites.statement: Apply the four operations to fractions and decimals confidently (from Lesson 4).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Ratios involving decimal or fractional terms (e.g. $0.6:1.5$ or $\tfrac23:\tfrac34$) and every step of the unitary method (dividing to find 'one part', then multiplying) depend directly on fluent fraction and decimal arithmetic.

prerequisites.statement: Understand what a fraction of a quantity means (from Lesson 4).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Correctly distinguishing 'B gets $\tfrac35$ of the total' from 'the ratio is $3:5$' (a genuinely different statement) depends on already being secure in what a fraction of a quantity represents.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide decimals accurately (e.g. $37.5\times8.50$ or $250\div1.17$), without a calculator or a written slip.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every rate calculation in this lesson is a single multiplication or division; the rate ideas themselves are simple, but an arithmetic slip in the decimal multiplication is the most common way to lose the mark.

prerequisites.statement: Convert a fraction of an hour to minutes and back, knowing that $1$ hour $=60$ minutes.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Time is the one quantity in this lesson that is not decimal: $3$ h $45$ min must become $3.75$ h before it can be used in speed $=$ distance $\div$ time, and this conversion step is where most speed questions actually go wrong.

prerequisites.statement: Rearrange a simple formula connecting three quantities (e.g. from $\text{speed}=\text{distance}\div\text{time}$ to $\text{time}=\text{distance}\div\text{speed}$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The speed/distance/time triangle and the density/pressure formulas are each used in three directions depending on which quantity is unknown; without this skill the triangle is just a picture with no way to use it.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise and keep track of units through a calculation (e.g. cm, m, km; g, kg; minutes, hours).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A rate is only meaningful with its unit attached, and mixing units (such as minutes with a speed given in km/h) before converting is one of the most common sources of a wrong answer in this lesson.

prerequisites.statement: Convert fluently between a percentage, a decimal and a fraction (e.g. $35\%=0.35=\tfrac{35}{100}$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every calculation in this lesson starts by turning a percentage into a decimal multiplier; without this conversion step the whole multiplier method cannot get started.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide decimals accurately, including with a calculator.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Once the percentage is written as a decimal, finding a percentage of an amount, increasing/decreasing a value, or reversing a percentage are all single multiplications or divisions, so an arithmetic slip here is the most common cause of a wrong final answer.

prerequisites.statement: Identify which of two quantities in a word problem is the 'whole' (the $100\%$ amount) and which is the 'part'.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every percentage statement is really a statement about $100\%$ of something; choosing the wrong quantity as the whole (for example the selling price instead of the cost price for a profit question) gives a plausible-looking but wrong answer.

prerequisites.statement: Round a money answer correctly to $2$ decimal places.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Almost every worked context in this lesson is money, and the exam expects money answers rounded to the nearest penny/cent, not left as a long decimal or rounded to $3$ significant figures.

prerequisites.statement: Convert a percentage to a decimal multiplier and use it to increase or decrease a quantity (from the previous Percentages lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every calculation in this lesson — currency, wages, profit, and both kinds of interest — is built from the SAME multiplier idea; without it, compound interest in particular has no way to get started.

prerequisites.statement: Use a power/index on a calculator (e.g. evaluate $1.025^3$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Compound interest over several years is calculated with a single power of the multiplier; without this calculator skill, a student is forced back into a slow year-by-year table even when a direct calculation is expected.

prerequisites.statement: Round a money answer to $2$ decimal places (the nearest cent or penny).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every answer in this lesson is a sum of money, and the exam expects the final answer rounded correctly, with the FULL calculator value carried through the working rather than a rounded intermediate value.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise that percentage profit/loss is measured against the cost price (from the previous Percentages lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson's profit and discount examples reuse that convention directly; without it, 'percentage profit' has no fixed meaning and could be measured against either price given in a question.

prerequisites.statement: Convert a percentage increase or decrease into a decimal multiplier (from the Percentages lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The multiplier $b$ is the single building block of every calculation in this lesson; without it there is no way to even start the model $a\times b^n$.

prerequisites.statement: Use the compound-interest model $P\times(1+r/100)^n$ (from the Money, Simple and Compound Interest lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Exponential growth and decay are the SAME model as compound interest, written with a general starting value $a$ and multiplier $b$ instead of a principal and a rate; recognising this means almost nothing new has to be learned, only generalised.

prerequisites.statement: Evaluate a power and an $n$th root on a calculator (e.g. $1.03^{10}$ and $\sqrt[3]{0.614125}$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Predicting a future value needs a power; finding an unknown rate needs the matching root — without fluent calculator use for both, neither direction of this lesson's work is possible.

prerequisites.statement: Build and read a simple table of values from a rule (e.g. substitute $n=1,2,3,\ldots$ into an expression).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding an unknown number of periods by trial and improvement means generating successive values in a table and reading off where the target is crossed; without this skill, the search has no organised method.

prerequisites.statement: Add and subtract whole numbers fluently, including carrying between place values.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The counting-up method for durations and every clock calculation in this lesson is built from careful addition and subtraction in base $60$ and base $24$; without fluent carrying, a time calculation collapses into decimal-style subtraction errors.

prerequisites.statement: Convert between a fraction or decimal and a related quantity (e.g. recognise that $0.25$ of something is one quarter of it).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Decimal hours are fractions of an hour in disguise ($0.75$ h $=45$ min); without this link, a calculator's decimal output cannot be translated back into minutes.

prerequisites.statement: Read values from a table with rows and columns (from earlier lessons).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Timetables are read exactly like any other table: matching a row (a stop) with a column (a particular train or bus) to find a single time.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise and use $\text{speed}=\text{distance}\div\text{time}$ (from the Rates lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several problems in this lesson give a duration and a distance and ask for a speed; the duration must first be converted into a decimal number of hours before the Rates formula can be applied at all.

prerequisites.statement: Apply the order of operations (brackets, powers, multiplication/division, addition/subtraction) to a numerical expression.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A calculator follows this order automatically, so knowing it is the only way to predict what the calculator WILL do, and to spot when an unbracketed expression will be evaluated differently from what was intended.

prerequisites.statement: Convert between decimal hours and hours-and-minutes notation (from the Time lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Entering a time correctly on a calculator means converting it to decimal hours first ($2$ h $30$ min $=2.5$ h); without this skill from the Time lesson, every time-based calculator calculation in this lesson starts from a wrong number.

prerequisites.statement: Write a number in standard form, $a\times10^n$ with $1\le a<10$ (from earlier in this unit).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Reading and entering a calculator's 'E' notation display correctly depends entirely on already knowing what standard form means and how the exponent affects the size of the number.

prerequisites.statement: Round a number to a given number of significant figures or decimal places.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This whole lesson is about WHEN to round (only at the very end); without already knowing HOW to round correctly, the final step of every calculation here cannot be completed accurately.

prerequisites.statement: List the factors, multiples or prime numbers below a given value (from earlier Number lessons).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Many sets in this lesson are described by a rule such as 'multiples of 3' or 'prime numbers', so listing a set correctly depends entirely on already being able to generate that list of numbers.

prerequisites.statement: Read and interpret an inequality such as $-2<x\le3$ on a number line.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Describing a set by a rule often uses exactly this inequality notation, and misreading an open or closed circle changes which numbers belong to the set.

prerequisites.statement: Add whole numbers fluently and check that several parts sum to a stated total.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every Venn-diagram counting problem is checked by confirming the numbers in all regions add up to $n(\xi)$; without reliable addition, an error in filling the diagram can go unnoticed.

prerequisites.statement: Express a simple probability as a fraction of favourable outcomes over the total number of outcomes.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several Venn-diagram problems finish by asking for the probability that a randomly chosen member of the universal set falls in a particular region, which is just the count in that region over $n(\xi)$.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise square numbers up to at least $144$ ($4,9,16,25,36,49,64,81,100,121,144$) and find factors of a number.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Simplifying a surd depends entirely on spotting the LARGEST square factor of the number under the root; without fluent recall of square numbers this becomes slow and error-prone guesswork.

prerequisites.statement: Expand a pair of brackets such as $(x+2)(x-3)$ using the distributive law.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Multiplying and expanding expressions with surds uses EXACTLY the same bracket-expansion method as algebra, just with $\sqrt{\ }$ in place of $x$; without this skill the expanding and rationalising sections cannot be followed.

prerequisites.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem, $a^2+b^2=c^2$, to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The geometry section of this lesson applies Pythagoras directly to sides given as surds, so without the theorem itself the exact-answer examples cannot be followed.

prerequisites.statement: Simplify a fraction by cancelling a common factor from the whole of the numerator and the whole of the denominator.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Rationalising a denominator finishes with exactly this kind of simplification, and a common error is cancelling only PART of a sum in the numerator rather than a genuine common factor of the whole thing.

prerequisites.statement: Carry out the four operations with negative numbers, including squaring a negative number.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every substitution in this lesson replaces a letter by a number that may be negative, and almost every common mistake in the lesson (sign errors, confusing $-a^2$ with $(-a)^2$) is really an arithmetic slip with negative numbers wearing an algebra costume.

prerequisites.statement: Apply the order of operations (brackets, powers, multiplication/division, addition/subtraction) to a numerical calculation.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Substitution is exactly 'apply the order of operations, but some of the numbers are hidden behind letters until you replace them'; without a secure order of operations, a correctly substituted expression can still be evaluated wrongly.

prerequisites.statement: Read a fraction bar as 'divided by', applying to everything above and below it.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Writing 'the sum of $a$ and $b$, halved' as $\dfrac{a+b}{2}$ rather than $\dfrac a2+b$ depends entirely on treating the fraction bar as a bracket around the whole numerator.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise a variable, a term and a coefficient, and substitute values into simple expressions (Lesson 2.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every rule in this lesson is justified by checking it with a substituted number; without fluent substitution, 'check by substituting $x=2$' is not available as a verification tool.

prerequisites.statement: Find the highest common factor (HCF) of two or more whole numbers.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Factorising by taking out a common factor is exactly 'find the HCF of the coefficients, and the lowest shared power of each letter' — the numerical half of the skill is pure HCF.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and add/subtract directed (positive and negative) numbers confidently.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A minus sign in front of a bracket changes the sign of every term inside it; this is simply 'multiplying by $-1$' applied term by term, and every sign error in expanding or factorising traces back to directed-number arithmetic.

prerequisites.statement: Factorise an expression completely by taking out a common factor (Lesson 2.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every method in this lesson begins with 'take out any common factor first'; skipping this step is the single most common reason a correct further factorisation ends up incomplete.

prerequisites.statement: Expand a product of two brackets, including $(x+a)^2$ and $(x+a)(x-a)$ (Lesson 2.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every factorising pattern in this lesson is the matching expansion pattern read backwards, and 'check by expanding' is the main verification tool used throughout.

prerequisites.statement: List the factor pairs of a positive or negative integer and test their sums.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding 'two numbers with a given product and a given sum' is the core engine of factorising both $x^2+bx+c$ and $ax^2+bx+c$.

prerequisites.statement: Expand $(x+p)^2$ and a product $a(x+p)^2$ fully (Lesson 2.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every completed-square answer is checked by expanding it back to the original quadratic; without fluent expansion, this verification step is unavailable.

prerequisites.statement: Understand that a squared real number is never negative.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The entire 'prove this expression is always positive' skill, and the fact that the vertex of $a(x+p)^2+q$ is a true minimum (for $a>0$) or maximum (for $a<0$), rests on $(\text{anything})^2\ge0$.

prerequisites.statement: Simplify a surd and halve a fraction, including an odd numerator (e.g. half of $3$ is $\tfrac32$, and $\left(\tfrac32\right)^2=\tfrac94$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Completing the square always starts by halving the coefficient of $x$, and this coefficient is frequently odd, so working confidently with the resulting fractions is essential throughout the lesson.

prerequisites.statement: Factorise a quadratic expression completely, including common factor, difference of squares, and trinomial factorisation (Lessons 2.2 and 2.3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every algebraic fraction skill in this lesson begins by factorising the numerator and denominator; without this, no factor is ever visible to cancel.

prerequisites.statement: Simplify a numeric fraction by cancelling a common factor, and understand that $\dfrac ab=\dfrac{ac}{bc}$ for $c\neq0$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Algebraic fractions obey exactly the same rule; the only new difficulty is that the factor being cancelled is an expression rather than a number.

prerequisites.statement: Expand a bracket preceded by a negative sign, e.g. $-2(x-2)=-2x+4$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Subtracting algebraic fractions always requires placing the second numerator in brackets and expanding it correctly; a sign error here is the single most common mistake when combining fractions.

prerequisites.statement: Use the laws of indices with numbers (e.g. $2^3\times2^4=2^7$) from the Number topic.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson applies exactly the same laws to algebraic terms; without fluency with numerical indices first, the algebraic generalisation has nothing to build on.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide algebraic terms with coefficients and letters, e.g. $3a^2\times4a^5$ (Lesson 2.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every simplification in this lesson splits into 'deal with the numbers' and 'deal with each letter separately', and the letter part is exactly this prerequisite skill with an index law layered on top.

prerequisites.statement: Find a square root and a cube root of a number by recognising perfect squares/cubes (e.g. $\sqrt[3]{27}=3$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Evaluating a fractional index always begins with taking a root; without recognising perfect $n$th powers quickly, this step becomes guesswork.

prerequisites.statement: Expand a single bracket and a bracket preceded by a negative sign (Lesson 2.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Almost every equation with brackets in this lesson begins by expanding them; without this, the equation cannot be reduced to the simple collect-and-divide form the balance method needs.

prerequisites.statement: Collect like terms, including terms with a negative coefficient.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Once brackets are expanded, every equation-solving step depends on correctly moving and combining $x$-terms and number terms.

prerequisites.statement: Find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of two small numbers.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Clearing fractions from an equation requires multiplying every term by the LCM of the denominators; without this, the fractions cannot be removed cleanly.

prerequisites.statement: Write an algebraic expression from a worded description, handling order-sensitive phrases such as 'less than', and tell an expression, an equation and a formula apart (Lesson 2.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every word problem in this lesson starts by turning English into algebra; a reversed subtraction or a confusion between an expression and an equation makes the equation wrong before any solving begins.

prerequisites.statement: Combine and simplify algebraic fractions using a common denominator, and factorise before cancelling (Lesson 2.5).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every fractional equation in this lesson is built from the same combining skill; recognising the common denominator is the first and most important step in clearing fractions from an equation.

prerequisites.statement: Factorise a quadratic expression, and use the quadratic formula $x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ when it does not factorise with integers.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Many fractional equations reduce to a quadratic equation once the fractions are cleared; this lesson assumes the quadratic can already be solved, and focuses on the new skill of getting to that quadratic correctly.

prerequisites.statement: Solve a linear equation using the balance method, including expanding brackets and collecting like terms (Lesson 2.7).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several fractional equations in this lesson reduce to a LINEAR equation after clearing fractions, and the final steps are solved exactly as in Lesson 2.7.

prerequisites.statement: Solve a linear equation in one unknown using the balance method (Lesson 2.7).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Both elimination and substitution eventually reduce a system of two equations to a single linear equation in one unknown, solved exactly as in Lesson 2.7.

prerequisites.statement: Expand brackets and clear fractions by multiplying every term by a common multiple (Lessons 2.2 and 2.7).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several systems in this lesson present an equation with brackets or fractions, which must be tidied into the standard $ax+by=c$ form before elimination or substitution can begin.

prerequisites.statement: Plot and read coordinates of a straight-line graph.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The graphical meaning of a simultaneous solution (the intersection point of two lines) only makes sense once straight-line graphs themselves are understood.

prerequisites.statement: Factorise a quadratic expression $x^2+bx+c$ and $ax^2+bx+c$ with $a\neq1$, including the ac-method of splitting the middle term (Lessons 2.2 and 2.3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Factorising a quadratic EXPRESSION and solving a quadratic EQUATION are almost the same calculation; this lesson's factorising method begins exactly where those earlier lessons left off.

prerequisites.statement: Complete the square on $x^2+bx+c$ and $ax^2+bx+c$, and find the vertex of $y=a(x+p)^2+q$ (Lesson 2.4).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson reuses the completing-the-square calculation directly, adding only the new final step of taking a square root of both sides to solve an equation.

prerequisites.statement: Simplify a surd, e.g. $\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5$, and recognise that a square root produces two signed values.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Both completing the square and the quadratic formula frequently produce an un-simplified surd that must be reduced, and both require remembering the $\pm$ sign to capture both roots.

nodes.title: Simultaneous Equations: One Linear, One Non-Linear

prerequisites.statement: Solve a quadratic equation $ax^2+bx+c=0$ by factorising and by the quadratic formula $x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every method in this lesson ends with a quadratic equation; without a reliable way to solve it (factorising when possible, the formula otherwise), the substitution step is wasted.

prerequisites.statement: Make a letter the subject of a simple linear formula (e.g. rearrange $x+y=5$ to $y=5-x$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The first step of every question here is rearranging the linear equation; getting this step wrong corrupts the substitution that follows.

prerequisites.statement: Expand a squared bracket correctly: $(a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2$, not $a^2-b^2$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Substituting a rearranged linear expression into a circle equation or a quadratic always produces a squared bracket; expanding it wrongly is the single most common failure point in this lesson.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise the equation of a circle centred at the origin, $x^2+y^2=r^2$, and that $r^2$ is the square of the radius.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several worked examples and exercises are a line meeting a circle; without this recognition the equation $x^2+y^2=17$ looks arbitrary rather than a circle of radius $\sqrt{17}$.

nodes.title: Changing the Subject of a Formula

prerequisites.statement: Solve a simple linear equation such as $2x+5=17$ by undoing operations with inverses (add/subtract, multiply/divide).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Changing the subject is exactly the same skill as solving a linear equation, except the numbers are replaced by letters — every inverse-operation step used here is one already practised on numerical equations.

prerequisites.statement: Expand a bracket such as $h(a+b)$ and factorise an expression with a common factor, such as $ab-3a=a(b-3)$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Both the bracket-based Core examples and every Extended 'subject appears twice' question depend on being able to expand a product and then factorise the wanted letter back out of a sum.

prerequisites.statement: Understand squaring and square-rooting (and cubing and cube-rooting) as a pair of inverse operations, and evaluate simple roots such as $\sqrt{25}=5$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The whole Extended section on powers and roots depends on recognising that 'square' and 'square root' undo each other, in exactly the same way 'add' and 'subtract' do.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute given numbers into a formula and evaluate it correctly, following the order of operations.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The recommended way to check a rearranged formula is to substitute numbers into both the original and the rearranged version; without reliable substitution, that check cannot be trusted.

prerequisites.statement: Order positive and negative numbers, and place them correctly on a number line.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every circle-and-line picture in this lesson depends on knowing exactly where a number such as $-3$ sits relative to $-1$ or $2$ on the line.

prerequisites.statement: Solve a linear equation such as $5-2x=11$ by undoing operations with inverses, including expanding a bracket such as $4(x+1)$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Solving a linear inequality uses exactly the same steps as solving the corresponding equation — the only new idea is the one extra rule about reversing the sign.

prerequisites.statement: Find the equation of a straight line in the form $y=mx+c$ from its gradient and intercept, or from two points on it.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Writing down the inequalities that define a shaded region (Extended) requires first finding the equation of each boundary line exactly as for any straight-line graph.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute coordinates into an expression such as $2x+y$ and evaluate the result.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Deciding which side of a boundary line is wanted always comes down to substituting a test point's coordinates into the inequality and evaluating whether the result is true.

prerequisites.statement: Find the difference between consecutive terms of a numerical pattern, and recognise a constant difference.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every method in this lesson — linear, quadratic or exponential — starts by looking at how the terms change from one to the next, so spotting and computing differences reliably comes first.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute a positive integer into an algebraic expression such as $n^2+3n$ or $2n-1$ and evaluate it correctly.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Checking a candidate $n$th term formula, and evaluating it to find a specific term, both depend entirely on reliable substitution.

prerequisites.statement: Solve a simple linear equation such as $4n+1=61$ for $n$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding WHICH term a given number is, or whether it is a term at all, always comes down to solving $T_n=\text{number}$ for $n$.

prerequisites.statement: Evaluate powers such as $2^4$, $3^3$ or $5^2$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Recognising and building formulas for square, cube and exponential sequences all require comfortably evaluating powers of small integers.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute given values into a formula and solve for an unknown constant, and rearrange a simple formula to change its subject.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every proportion question follows the same shape — substitute a known pair to find $k$, then substitute again to find an unknown — so reliable substitution and rearrangement underlie the entire lesson.

prerequisites.statement: Evaluate and manipulate powers, square roots and cube roots of numbers, e.g. $3^3=27$, $\sqrt{16}=4$, $\sqrt[3]{125}=5$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every type of proportion in this lesson is built from a power or a root of $x$, so comfortably working with powers and roots in both directions is needed throughout.

prerequisites.statement: Solve an equation in which the unknown is raised to a power or is under a root, such as $2x^2=32$ or $k\sqrt x=8$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The last step of nearly every proportion question is exactly this kind of equation, obtained after substituting the known constant $k$.

prerequisites.statement: Convert a percentage change into a multiplying decimal factor, e.g. 'increase by $20\%$' means multiply by $1.2$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding the effect of a percentage change in $x$ on $y$, without finding $k$, depends entirely on this conversion.

prerequisites.statement: Find the gradient of a straight line from two points on it, $\dfrac{\text{change in }y}{\text{change in }x}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every rate read from a practical graph in this lesson — speed, acceleration, price per kilometre, litres per minute — is found exactly this way: a gradient calculation on the graph.

prerequisites.statement: Rearrange and use the formula $\text{speed}=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$ with consistent units.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Distance-time and speed-time graphs are visual versions of exactly this formula, so fluency with it underlies every reading taken from either kind of graph.

prerequisites.statement: Find the area of a triangle ($\tfrac12bh$) and a trapezium ($\tfrac12(a+b)h$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Distance travelled on a speed-time graph is read as the area under the graph, which for straight-line sections is always a triangle, a rectangle or a trapezium.

prerequisites.statement: Convert between related units using a multiplying or dividing factor, e.g. hours to minutes, or metres per second to kilometres per hour.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several practical questions mix units (hours and minutes, m/s and km/h), and getting a rate right depends on consistent unit conversion before or after reading the graph.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute a value into an algebraic expression, including negative numbers, to evaluate it correctly.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every table of values in this lesson is built one substitution at a time, and a sign slip in a single entry throws off the whole curve.

prerequisites.statement: Solve a quadratic equation by factorising, $x^2+bx+c=(x+p)(x+q)$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Checking a graphical root against its exact algebraic value (and solving the intersection equations in the challenge problems) both need this skill.

prerequisites.statement: Plot coordinates accurately on a pair of axes and read values from a graph.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson is built entirely on plotting points, drawing curves through them, and reading values back off the finished graph.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise the equation of a straight line $y=mx+c$ and identify its gradient $m$ and $y$-intercept $c$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several of this lesson's graphical solutions involve drawing a straight line alongside a curve, which requires finding and plotting that line correctly first.

prerequisites.statement: Factorise a quadratic expression $x^2+bx+c=(x+p)(x+q)$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding the roots of a quadratic or cubic by factorising is the fastest route to the $x$-intercepts needed for every sketch in this lesson.

prerequisites.statement: Expand a bracket such as $(x+p)^2$ or $(x-a)(x-b)$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Completing the square and checking a turning point both rely on being able to expand a squared bracket back out and compare it with the original expression.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute a value into an algebraic expression, including negative numbers.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every $y$-intercept, turning-point value and intercept check in this lesson is a single substitution, and a sign slip there produces a wrongly placed sketch.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise the shapes of plotted linear, quadratic, reciprocal and exponential graphs from a table of values (as drawn with a grid and scale in the previous lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Sketching trades the grid and the table for direct recognition of the same shapes from the equation alone, so this lesson builds directly on having already seen each shape plotted accurately.

prerequisites.statement: Find the gradient of a straight line from two points on it, $\dfrac{\text{change in }y}{\text{change in }x}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Estimating the gradient of a curve at a point starts by finding the gradient of its tangent, which is itself just a straight line through two chosen points.

prerequisites.statement: Expand brackets, such as $(x+p)(x+q)$, and collect like terms.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A function given as a product of brackets must be expanded into a sum of powers of $x$ before the differentiation rule for $ax^n$ can be applied to it.

prerequisites.statement: Factorise a quadratic expression $x^2+bx+c=(x+p)(x+q)$, and solve a quadratic equation.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Solving $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$ to find stationary points almost always means factorising and solving a quadratic equation in $x$.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute a value into an algebraic expression, including negative numbers.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every gradient-at-a-point calculation, every stationary-point $y$-value, and every second-derivative test in this lesson is a substitution, and a sign slip there gives a wrong classification.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute a value, including a negative number or an algebraic expression such as $2a$, into a given rule.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Evaluating $\mathrm f(x)$ for any input, including an algebraic one like $\mathrm f(2a)$, is pure substitution; a slip here propagates into every later section of the lesson.

prerequisites.statement: Solve a linear equation, and a simple equation of the form $x^2=k$ (giving two roots when $k>0$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Solving $\mathrm f(x)=10$ or $\mathrm h(x)=53$ for $x$ is just solving the equation that results, and a squared rule gives two solutions that must both be reported.

prerequisites.statement: Rearrange a formula to make a chosen letter the subject, including when that letter appears inside a fraction or on both sides.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding $\mathrm f^{-1}(x)$ is exactly this rearrangement skill, applied to $y=\mathrm f(x)$; a fractional function needs the extra step of collecting all the $x$-terms together first.

prerequisites.statement: Plot and read coordinates on a pair of axes, and recognise that reflecting the point $(a,b)$ in the line $y=x$ gives $(b,a)$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding a range from a sketch, and relating the graphs of $\mathrm f$ and $\mathrm f^{-1}$, both depend on reading a graph accurately and on this specific reflection fact.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute a positive or negative number into a simple algebraic expression, such as finding $2x-1$ when $x=-2$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every table of values in this lesson is built by substituting a chosen $x$ into an equation; without reliable substitution, including with negative numbers, the table (and so the whole graph) will carry arithmetic errors forward.

prerequisites.statement: Understand that on a number line, negative numbers lie to the left of zero (or below it, for a vertical line).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Reading and plotting coordinates such as $(-4,-1)$ depends on correctly interpreting negative distances as steps left or down from the origin, not just 'small' numbers.

prerequisites.statement: Solve a simple one-step linear equation, such as $2k=-8$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding a missing coordinate (e.g. the value of $k$ so that $(k,-9)$ lies on a given line) always ends in a one-step equation that must be solved for the unknown.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise and simplify a fraction such as $\tfrac53$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The intercept method (Extended) frequently produces intercepts that are not whole numbers, e.g. $x=\tfrac53$, and these must be read and plotted sensibly rather than ignored or rounded without reason.

prerequisites.statement: Plot and read coordinates $(x,y)$ in all four quadrants, and recognise $x=k$ and $y=k$ as vertical and horizontal lines.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A gradient triangle is built from two points on a line, and recognising a zero or undefined gradient depends directly on recognising horizontal and vertical lines from the previous lesson.

prerequisites.statement: Simplify a fraction, such as $\tfrac{6}{4}$, to its lowest terms, and subtract negative numbers, such as $-1-3$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every gradient calculation ends in a fraction $\tfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}$ that should be simplified, and both the rise and the run are found by subtracting coordinates that are frequently negative.

prerequisites.statement: Understand that division by zero is undefined.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A vertical line's gradient calculation always ends with a zero run in the denominator, and recognising why this makes the gradient 'undefined' (rather than zero, or some very large number) depends on this fact.

prerequisites.statement: Find the gradient of a line, either by reading a grid or from the coordinates of two points.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every method of finding an equation in this lesson — from a graph or from two points — begins by finding the gradient $m$ exactly as in the previous lesson, before any new skill is applied.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute a pair of coordinates into an equation and solve the resulting one-step equation for an unknown constant.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding $c$ in $y=mx+c$, once $m$ is known, is always a substitute-and-solve step using one point's coordinates.

prerequisites.statement: Rearrange a simple equation to make a chosen letter the subject, such as turning $2y=6x-8$ into $y=3x-4$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Reading the gradient and intercept from a line given as $ax+by=c$ (Extended) is impossible without first rearranging it into $y=mx+c$ form.

nodes.title: Length and Midpoint of a Line Segment

prerequisites.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem, $a^2+b^2=c^2$, to find the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle from its two shorter sides.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The distance formula IS Pythagoras' theorem applied to the horizontal and vertical differences between two points; without it, the formula is just a rule to memorise rather than something understood.

prerequisites.statement: Find the average of two numbers, such as $\dfrac{-3+9}{2}$, including when one or both are negative.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The midpoint formula finds the average of the two $x$-coordinates and the average of the two $y$-coordinates separately; every midpoint calculation is two averages side by side.

prerequisites.statement: Simplify a surd, such as writing $\sqrt{20}$ as $2\sqrt5$, and round a decimal to $3$ significant figures.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A distance is rarely a whole number; the IGCSE convention is to leave it as an exact surd when asked, or round to $3$ s.f. otherwise, and both skills are needed to give a correctly-formatted final answer.

prerequisites.statement: Apply the converse of Pythagoras' theorem: if $a^2+b^2=c^2$ for a triangle's three sides, the angle opposite the longest side is a right angle.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Showing a triangle found from coordinates is right-angled relies entirely on this converse statement, applied to the three squared lengths found with the distance formula.

prerequisites.statement: Read the gradient $m$ and $y$-intercept $c$ from an equation in the form $y=mx+c$, rearranging first if necessary.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Deciding whether two lines are parallel always starts by comparing their gradients, which can only be read off correctly once each equation is in, or rearranged into, $y=mx+c$ form.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute a point's coordinates into $y=mx+c$ and solve the resulting equation for $c$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding the equation of a new line parallel to a given one, through a given point, is exactly this substitute-and-solve step, once the shared gradient has been identified.

prerequisites.statement: Rearrange $ax+by=c$ into $y=mx+c$ form.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Testing whether two lines given in the form $ax+by=c$ are parallel, or finding a new line parallel to one, depends on first extracting each line's gradient by rearranging.

prerequisites.statement: Find the gradient of a line segment from two points using $m=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The negative-reciprocal condition for perpendicularity is applied directly to gradients, so a gradient must first be found correctly from any two points given.

prerequisites.statement: Find the midpoint of a line segment using $\left(\tfrac{x_1+x_2}2,\tfrac{y_1+y_2}2\right)$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The perpendicular bisector of a segment must pass through its midpoint, so this earlier skill is combined directly with the new perpendicular-gradient rule.

prerequisites.statement: Find the equation of a line through a given point with a given gradient, substituting into $y=mx+c$ to solve for $c$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Once the perpendicular gradient is found, constructing the actual equation of the new line uses exactly this substitute-and-solve step.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise and name basic 2D shapes (triangle, square, rectangle, circle) and basic 3D solids (cube, sphere) from earlier years.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson sorts those familiar shapes into precise families (by sides, by angles) and adds the exact vocabulary a mark scheme expects; without the shapes already being familiar by sight, the new vocabulary has nothing to attach to.

prerequisites.statement: Add and subtract numbers up to a few hundred, including with a calculator-free method.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Angle facts such as 'interior + exterior = $180^{\circ}$' and 'a full turn is $360^{\circ}$' are used immediately in worked examples and exercises, and every one of them is a simple addition or subtraction.

prerequisites.statement: Understand that a fraction such as $\tfrac12$ or a ratio such as $2:1$ describes 'how many times bigger'.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The scale factor that distinguishes similar shapes from congruent ones is exactly this idea applied to lengths; without it, 'similar' can only be learned as a disconnected new word.

prerequisites.statement: Plot and read coordinates $(x,y)$ on a pair of axes.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The Extended exercise on the perpendicular bisector of a segment $AB$ given by coordinates needs the midpoint and the idea of a vertical or horizontal line as an equation.

prerequisites.statement: Name and recognise triangles, special quadrilaterals, polygons and common 3D solids (lesson 4.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every construction and every net in this lesson is built from these exact named shapes (triangles, rhombi, squares, cuboids, prisms, pyramids); without the names already secure, the instructions in this lesson have nothing to refer to.

prerequisites.statement: Find the area of a rectangle ($\text{length}\times\text{width}$) and of a triangle ($\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every surface-area calculation in this lesson is just adding up the areas of the rectangles and triangles that make up a net, so these two area formulas are used in every single worked example on surface area.

prerequisites.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem $a^2+b^2=c^2$ to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The rhombus-diagonal and square pyramid examples both need a right-angled triangle's third side (half-diagonal, or perpendicular height from slant height and half the base) before the main calculation can even start; Pythagoras' theorem itself is formalised fully in a later unit, but the IGCSE course assumes it is already usable here.

prerequisites.statement: Convert between millimetres, centimetres and metres, and use a percentage increase as a multiplier (e.g. adding $10\%$ means multiplying by $1.1$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Measuring to the nearest millimetre, and the cereal-box exercise's '$10\%$ extra for glue flaps', both depend on comfortable unit and percentage conversion.

prerequisites.statement: Work with ratios and simplify or scale them, and convert confidently between millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every scale calculation is a ratio multiplication or division, and the single most common slip in this topic is an un-converted unit left in centimetres when the answer should be in metres or kilometres.

prerequisites.statement: Measure and draw lines to the nearest millimetre and angles to the nearest degree with a ruler and protractor (lesson 4.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A scale drawing or a bearing diagram is only as accurate as the measuring and drawing skill behind it; every worked example in this lesson assumes that skill is already secure.

prerequisites.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem and the tangent ratio to find a missing side or angle of a right-angled triangle.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several worked examples and most of the challenge problems check a scale-drawing answer by an exact calculation (e.g. $\sqrt{6^2+8^2}$ for a distance, $\tan^{-1}(6/8)$ for a bearing); the full trigonometry unit comes later, but these two tools are assumed usable now exactly as lesson 4.2 already assumed Pythagoras.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise the four cardinal points (N, E, S, W) and the four intercardinal points (NE, SE, SW, NW).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several practice questions ask for the bearing of a compass direction directly, and the compass rose is the mental anchor for estimating whether a measured bearing is plausible.

prerequisites.statement: Work with ratios and proportion, including finding an unknown quantity from a known ratio (e.g. solving $\frac{x}{9}=\frac{8}{6}$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every single calculation in this lesson is 'find the scale factor, then multiply or divide by it' — the whole lesson is an application of proportional reasoning to geometric figures.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise vertically opposite angles, corresponding and alternate angles on parallel lines, and that the angles of a triangle add to $180^{\circ}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every 'show that two triangles are similar' argument in this lesson relies on naming one of these angle facts as the reason for a pair of equal angles; the full formal treatment of angle facts comes in lesson 4.6, but these specific facts are assumed already familiar from earlier years, exactly as this lesson's own worked examples use them without re-deriving them.

prerequisites.statement: Find the area of a square or triangle, and the volume of a cube or cuboid.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The $k^2$/$k^3$ relationships are introduced by directly comparing the area of a unit square with a $k$-times-larger square, and the volume of a unit cube with a $k$-times-larger cube; without these basic formulas already secure, that comparison has nothing to stand on.

prerequisites.statement: Name corresponding sides, angles and vertices between two shapes described with matching vertex letters (e.g. $P\leftrightarrow A$, $Q\leftrightarrow B$) (lesson 4.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every similarity calculation depends on correctly pairing up corresponding sides; without this naming skill secure, the scale factor itself cannot be set up correctly.

prerequisites.statement: Name and recognise common 2D shapes: triangle types, special quadrilaterals, and regular polygons (lesson 4.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every statement in this lesson ('a rhombus has 2 lines of symmetry', 'a kite has order 1') refers to these shapes by name; without the vocabulary secure, the statements have nothing to attach to.

prerequisites.statement: Plot coordinate points, find the gradient between two points, and find the distance between two points.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The 'completing a symmetric shape' worked example uses all three skills directly: finding the mirror line's equation from a gradient, reflecting a point in that line, and checking the result with a distance calculation.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise common 3D solids by name: prisms, cylinders, pyramids and cones (lesson 4.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The Extended section names and counts planes/axes for exactly these solids; without the solids already named and pictured correctly, 'a plane parallel to the circular ends' has no solid to attach to.

prerequisites.statement: Know that a full turn is $360^{\circ}$ and a right angle is $90^{\circ}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The order of rotational symmetry is defined directly in terms of $360^{\circ}$ (smallest fitting turn $=360^{\circ}\div n$), and several exercises work backwards from a given angle to find $n$.

prerequisites.statement: Name and recognise triangle types, special quadrilaterals and polygons (lesson 4.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every angle fact in this lesson is stated in terms of a named shape ('isosceles triangle', 'quadrilateral', 'regular polygon'); without the vocabulary secure, the facts cannot even be matched to a diagram.

prerequisites.statement: Set up and solve a simple linear equation, including one with the unknown on both sides (e.g. $3a+10=5a-30$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Nearly every exercise in this lesson ends in an equation like 'angles add up to a known total, find $x$'; without equation-solving secure, the geometry reasoning cannot be converted into a numeric answer.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise the arrowhead marking convention for parallel lines on a diagram.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every parallel-lines angle fact in this lesson depends on first confirming, from the diagram's arrowheads, that the two lines genuinely are marked parallel — these facts are invalid otherwise.

prerequisites.statement: Divide a quantity in a given ratio (e.g. split $180^{\circ}$ in the ratio $2:3:4$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: At least one standard exercise states a triangle's angles as a ratio directly, which needs ratio division (not just an equation) to convert into actual angle sizes.

prerequisites.statement: Apply basic angle facts (angles on a line, angles in a triangle, vertically opposite angles, base angles of an isosceles triangle) and give reasons (lesson 4.6).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every circle-theorem proof and every multi-step exercise in this lesson chains a circle fact together with an ordinary angle fact (most often the triangle angle sum or isosceles base angles); without these secure, a circle-theorem argument cannot be completed.

prerequisites.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Once the tangent-radius theorem establishes a right angle, several problems (finding a tangent length, or the distance from an external point to the centre) are completed with Pythagoras, not with any further circle fact.

prerequisites.statement: Set up and solve a simple linear equation.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Cyclic-quadrilateral problems routinely state two opposite angles as algebraic expressions and ask you to find the unknown by solving an equation from the $180^{\circ}$ fact.

prerequisites.statement: Use the sine and cosine ratios in a right-angled triangle (formally taught in the Trigonometry unit).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: One challenge problem (finding chord lengths from a diameter and an angle, using the semicircle theorem) needs a sine or cosine ratio. Trigonometry is taught formally in its own unit; if you have not met it yet, you can leave that problem until later.

prerequisites.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every property in this lesson (chord-distance, equal chords, tangent length) produces a right-angled triangle, and Pythagoras' theorem is the tool that turns that triangle into a numeric answer in almost every exercise.

prerequisites.statement: Use the fact that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact (lesson 4.7).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The tangent-length theorem and every tangent-related right-angled triangle in this lesson depends directly on this one fact from the previous lesson to establish the right angle in the first place.

prerequisites.statement: Use the sine, cosine and tangent ratios in a right-angled triangle (formally taught in the Trigonometry unit).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several problems (finding the angle between two tangents, or a chord's half-angle at the centre) need a trig ratio, not just Pythagoras. Trigonometry is taught formally in its own unit; if you have not met it yet, leave those problems until you have.

prerequisites.statement: Use the fact that base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal (lesson 4.6).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Both the radii-to-a-chord triangle and the tangent kite are built from isosceles triangles (equal radii; equal tangent lengths), and several angle-chasing steps depend on this fact.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide a number by 10, 100 and 1000 (and other powers of 10) mentally.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every metric conversion in this lesson is exactly a multiplication or division by a power of 10 (or, for area and volume, by that power of 10 squared or cubed); without fast, confident recall of this skill every conversion becomes a slow, error-prone calculation.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise that the area of a square of side 1 unit is exactly 1 square unit.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Seeing why 1 m$^2$ is a square of side 100 cm, and therefore holds $100\times100$ unit squares of 1 cm$^2$, is the entire justification for squaring the length factor when converting areas; without this picture, 'square the conversion factor' is just a rule to memorise, not something understood.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide decimals, including decimals less than 1.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several conversions in this lesson go from a larger unit to a smaller one and back (e.g. 250 g to kg, 0.85 L to ml), and these routinely produce or start from decimals.

prerequisites.statement: Find the volume of a cuboid as length × width × height.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several of this lesson's context problems (a tank, a swimming pool, rainfall on a roof) ask for a volume in one unit system before converting it to another; without the cuboid volume formula itself, there is nothing yet to convert.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise a right angle and identify when two line segments are perpendicular to each other.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every area formula in this lesson (triangle, parallelogram, trapezium) needs the PERPENDICULAR height, not a slanted side; without being able to spot a right angle in a diagram, the wrong length gets substituted every time.

prerequisites.statement: Solve a simple linear equation in one unknown, such as $2(2w+w)=30$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every 'working backwards' problem in this lesson (missing width, missing height, missing parallel side, algebraic sides) ends in exactly this kind of one-step or two-step equation.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide decimals, and substitute a number into a simple algebraic expression such as $2x+1$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Both the numerical substitutions (e.g. $A=\tfrac12\times9\times6$) and the algebraic-side problems in this lesson depend on comfortable substitution and arithmetic with decimals.

prerequisites.statement: Convert between units of length, such as between metres and centimetres (Lesson 5.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A handful of context problems in this lesson (fencing a lawn, painting a wall) only make sense once every length is already expressed in a single, consistent unit.

prerequisites.statement: Understand that $\pi$ is an irrational number: a fixed but never-ending, never-repeating decimal, and that $3.14$ and $\tfrac{22}{7}$ are only approximations to it.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every formula in this lesson is built around $\pi$; without knowing it is a genuine, exact constant (not a rounded value chosen for convenience), 'leave your answer in terms of $\pi$' makes no sense as an instruction.

prerequisites.statement: Find a simple fraction of $360$, such as $\tfrac{90}{360}=\tfrac14$ or $\tfrac{60}{360}=\tfrac16$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The entire idea of this lesson — that a sector is the fraction $\tfrac{\theta}{360}$ of a whole circle — depends on being able to simplify that fraction quickly and correctly.

prerequisites.statement: Rearrange a simple formula to make a different letter the subject, such as rearranging $y=kx$ to find $x$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding a missing radius from a circumference or area, or a missing angle from an arc length, is exactly this kind of rearrangement applied to the circle formulas.

prerequisites.statement: Convert between units of length, area and volume (Lesson 5.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Some context problems (wheels covering a distance, clock hands sweeping an area) mix units that must be made consistent before substituting into a circle formula.

prerequisites.statement: Find the area of a rectangle, triangle, trapezium and circle (Lessons 5.2 and 5.3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every prism's volume starts from the area of its cross-section, and a pyramid or cone's total surface area starts from the area of its base — without these area formulas on demand, no solid's volume or surface area can be built.

prerequisites.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A cone's slant height, a pyramid's slant height, and the vertical height recovered from a slant height are all found using $l^2=r^2+h^2$ or an equivalent right-angled triangle inside the solid.

prerequisites.statement: Convert between units of volume and capacity, such as $\text{cm}^3$ to litres (Lesson 5.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several context problems in this lesson (a tin's capacity, a tank's contents) ask for a final answer in litres or millilitres rather than $\text{cm}^3$.

prerequisites.statement: Take the cube root of a number, and recognise cubing as the inverse operation.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Finding a missing radius from a sphere's volume, or a missing side from a cube's volume, both require undoing a cube by taking a cube root.

nodes.title: Compound Shapes and Parts of Shapes

prerequisites.statement: Find the area and perimeter of a rectangle, triangle, trapezium and circle (or a part of one), and the volume and surface area of a prism, cylinder, cone, pyramid and sphere (Lessons 5.2, 5.3 and 5.4).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every compound shape or solid in this lesson is built by adding or subtracting these exact basic shapes, so each must already be available on demand.

prerequisites.statement: Use similar triangles to find a ratio of corresponding lengths.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A frustum's missing cone (the small cone that was sliced off) is recovered by scaling the large cone's dimensions down using a ratio found from similar triangles.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise a hemisphere as exactly half a sphere, and a half-cylinder as exactly half a cylinder.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A hemisphere's volume and curved surface area are both exactly half of the corresponding sphere's; forgetting this halving (or halving the wrong quantity) is a common first error when a compound solid includes one.

prerequisites.statement: Convert between units of volume and capacity, such as $\text{cm}^3$ to litres (Lesson 5.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several compound-solid context problems (a bucket, a tank) ask for a final answer in litres rather than $\text{cm}^3$.

prerequisites.statement: Square a number and find a square root with a calculator, including non-perfect squares.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every step of Pythagoras' theorem is either squaring a known side or square-rooting a sum of squares; without fluent squaring and rooting, the theorem cannot be applied even when the triangle is set up correctly.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise a right angle in a diagram and identify the three vertices and three sides of a triangle.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The whole theorem depends on first finding which angle is the right angle and which side is opposite it; this lesson gives no credit for correct arithmetic applied to the wrong side.

prerequisites.statement: Simplify a surd by finding its largest square factor, e.g. $\sqrt{72}=6\sqrt2$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several Extended-tier questions ask for an exact length rather than a decimal, and an unsimplified surd such as $\sqrt{72}$ is not accepted as a final 'simplest form' answer.

prerequisites.statement: Plot and read coordinates $(x,y)$ on a pair of axes, and find a horizontal or vertical difference between two points.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The distance-between-two-points formula is just Pythagoras' theorem applied to the horizontal and vertical differences; without comfort with coordinates, the formula is a meaningless string of letters.

prerequisites.statement: Identify the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle and know that the other two sides are the legs (from Lesson 6.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Naming the opposite and adjacent sides is only possible once the hypotenuse is already correctly identified; everything in this lesson is built on that first label.

prerequisites.statement: Rearrange a simple equation of the form $\sin\theta=\tfrac{x}{12}$ to make $x$, or $\theta$, the subject.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every 'find a side' or 'find an angle' question in this lesson reduces to rearranging one short equation; without comfortable algebra here, the correct trigonometric setup still leads to a wrong final answer.

prerequisites.statement: Use a scientific calculator to evaluate $\sin$, $\cos$, $\tan$ and their inverse functions in degree mode.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This is a purely mechanical skill, but a calculator left in radian or gradian mode silently produces a wrong answer with no error message, which is the single most common cause of a wrong trigonometry mark in the exam.

prerequisites.statement: Understand that bearings are measured clockwise from north and written with three figures (e.g. $065^{\circ}$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Bearings problems in this lesson assume this convention is already familiar; without it, a correctly drawn triangle can still be converted to the wrong final bearing.

nodes.title: Angles of Elevation, Depression and Shortest Distance

prerequisites.statement: Use SOH-CAH-TOA to find a side or an angle in a right-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every elevation/depression problem is a right-angled-triangle trigonometry problem in disguise; the new skill in this lesson is entirely about drawing the correct diagram, not about new trigonometric machinery.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise alternate angles between a pair of parallel lines cut by a transversal.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The equality 'angle of depression from A to B = angle of elevation from B to A' is proved directly by alternate angles between two parallel horizontal lines; without this, the equality must be memorised rather than understood.

prerequisites.statement: Rearrange and solve a linear equation in one unknown, including one with the unknown on both sides.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The two-observer method produces an equation such as $x\tan40^{\circ}=(x+30)\tan25^{\circ}$ with the unknown on both sides; without comfortable algebra here, the correct trigonometric setup cannot be finished.

prerequisites.statement: Find the area of a triangle using $\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The 'equal areas' method for the shortest distance from a point to a line, when only the triangle's three sides are known, relies directly on this formula.

prerequisites.statement: Use SOH-CAH-TOA to find a side or angle in a right-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson reuses the exact same ratios; the only change is that the triangle's sides are now expressed as simple numbers and surds instead of a decimal measurement.

prerequisites.statement: Simplify a surd and rationalise a denominator of the form $\dfrac{a}{\sqrt b}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every exact-value answer in this lesson is expected in simplified, rationalised form; without this skill a correct trigonometric setup still fails to produce an accepted final answer.

prerequisites.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle, including leaving the answer as an exact surd.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Both special triangles in this lesson (the half-square and the half-equilateral triangle) are built by applying Pythagoras' theorem to a triangle with simple whole-number sides.

prerequisites.statement: Expand a squared bracket such as $(a+b)^2$ and simplify the result.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several 'show that' exact-value questions require expanding a bracket containing surds and simplifying term by term; without this algebra skill, the trigonometric substitution alone is not enough to finish the question.

prerequisites.statement: Find an acute angle from $\sin,\cos$ or $\tan$ using a calculator's inverse functions (from Lesson 6.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The 'first' solution found by a calculator's inverse function is always the starting point from which every other solution on $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$ is generated using symmetry.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise the exact trigonometric values and how $\sin,\cos,\tan$ relate to a right-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.4).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The CAST diagram and the graphs extend the SAME three ratios beyond $90^{\circ}$; without a solid right-triangle picture of what $\sin,\cos,\tan$ mean, the extension to a full circle/graph has nothing to build on.

prerequisites.statement: Read coordinates and key features (intercepts, turning points, period) from a sketched graph.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The sine, cosine and tangent graphs are read and sketched using exactly this same graph vocabulary.

prerequisites.statement: Rearrange a simple linear equation, including one with a negative coefficient (e.g. $6-5c=9\Rightarrow c=-0.6$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several equations in this lesson must first be rearranged algebraically into the form $\sin x=k$ or $\tan x=k$ before the graph/CAST method can be applied.

nodes.title: Non-Right-Angled Triangles: The Sine and Cosine Rules

prerequisites.statement: Use SOH-CAH-TOA to find a side or angle in a RIGHT-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The sine and cosine rules are needed precisely because SOH-CAH-TOA only works when there is a right angle; recognising that absence is the trigger for using these new rules.

prerequisites.statement: Use the angle sum of a triangle ($180^{\circ}$) to find a missing angle.
