from.statement: Apply basic angle facts (angles on a line, angles in a triangle, vertically opposite angles, base angles of an isosceles triangle) and give reasons (lesson 4.6).
from.why_it_matters: Every circle-theorem proof and every multi-step exercise in this lesson chains a circle fact together with an ordinary angle fact (most often the triangle angle sum or isosceles base angles); without these secure, a circle-theorem argument cannot be completed.

from.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle.
from.why_it_matters: Once the tangent-radius theorem establishes a right angle, several problems (finding a tangent length, or the distance from an external point to the centre) are completed with Pythagoras, not with any further circle fact.

from.statement: Set up and solve a simple linear equation.
from.why_it_matters: Cyclic-quadrilateral problems routinely state two opposite angles as algebraic expressions and ask you to find the unknown by solving an equation from the $180^{\circ}$ fact.

from.statement: Use the sine and cosine ratios in a right-angled triangle (formally taught in the Trigonometry unit).
from.why_it_matters: One challenge problem (finding chord lengths from a diameter and an angle, using the semicircle theorem) needs a sine or cosine ratio. Trigonometry is taught formally in its own unit; if you have not met it yet, you can leave that problem until later.

from.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle.
from.why_it_matters: Every property in this lesson (chord-distance, equal chords, tangent length) produces a right-angled triangle, and Pythagoras' theorem is the tool that turns that triangle into a numeric answer in almost every exercise.

from.statement: Use the fact that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact (lesson 4.7).
from.why_it_matters: The tangent-length theorem and every tangent-related right-angled triangle in this lesson depends directly on this one fact from the previous lesson to establish the right angle in the first place.

from.statement: Use the sine, cosine and tangent ratios in a right-angled triangle (formally taught in the Trigonometry unit).
from.why_it_matters: Several problems (finding the angle between two tangents, or a chord's half-angle at the centre) need a trig ratio, not just Pythagoras. Trigonometry is taught formally in its own unit; if you have not met it yet, leave those problems until you have.

from.statement: Use the fact that base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal (lesson 4.6).
from.why_it_matters: Both the radii-to-a-chord triangle and the tangent kite are built from isosceles triangles (equal radii; equal tangent lengths), and several angle-chasing steps depend on this fact.

from.statement: Multiply and divide a number by 10, 100 and 1000 (and other powers of 10) mentally.
from.why_it_matters: Every metric conversion in this lesson is exactly a multiplication or division by a power of 10 (or, for area and volume, by that power of 10 squared or cubed); without fast, confident recall of this skill every conversion becomes a slow, error-prone calculation.

from.statement: Recognise that the area of a square of side 1 unit is exactly 1 square unit.
from.why_it_matters: Seeing why 1 m$^2$ is a square of side 100 cm, and therefore holds $100\times100$ unit squares of 1 cm$^2$, is the entire justification for squaring the length factor when converting areas; without this picture, 'square the conversion factor' is just a rule to memorise, not something understood.

from.statement: Multiply and divide decimals, including decimals less than 1.
from.why_it_matters: Several conversions in this lesson go from a larger unit to a smaller one and back (e.g. 250 g to kg, 0.85 L to ml), and these routinely produce or start from decimals.

from.statement: Find the volume of a cuboid as length × width × height.
from.why_it_matters: Several of this lesson's context problems (a tank, a swimming pool, rainfall on a roof) ask for a volume in one unit system before converting it to another; without the cuboid volume formula itself, there is nothing yet to convert.

from.statement: Recognise a right angle and identify when two line segments are perpendicular to each other.
from.why_it_matters: Every area formula in this lesson (triangle, parallelogram, trapezium) needs the PERPENDICULAR height, not a slanted side; without being able to spot a right angle in a diagram, the wrong length gets substituted every time.

from.statement: Solve a simple linear equation in one unknown, such as $2(2w+w)=30$.
from.why_it_matters: Every 'working backwards' problem in this lesson (missing width, missing height, missing parallel side, algebraic sides) ends in exactly this kind of one-step or two-step equation.

from.statement: Multiply and divide decimals, and substitute a number into a simple algebraic expression such as $2x+1$.
from.why_it_matters: Both the numerical substitutions (e.g. $A=\tfrac12\times9\times6$) and the algebraic-side problems in this lesson depend on comfortable substitution and arithmetic with decimals.

from.statement: Convert between units of length, such as between metres and centimetres (Lesson 5.1).
from.why_it_matters: A handful of context problems in this lesson (fencing a lawn, painting a wall) only make sense once every length is already expressed in a single, consistent unit.

from.statement: Understand that $\pi$ is an irrational number: a fixed but never-ending, never-repeating decimal, and that $3.14$ and $\tfrac{22}{7}$ are only approximations to it.
from.why_it_matters: Every formula in this lesson is built around $\pi$; without knowing it is a genuine, exact constant (not a rounded value chosen for convenience), 'leave your answer in terms of $\pi$' makes no sense as an instruction.

from.statement: Find a simple fraction of $360$, such as $\tfrac{90}{360}=\tfrac14$ or $\tfrac{60}{360}=\tfrac16$.
from.why_it_matters: The entire idea of this lesson — that a sector is the fraction $\tfrac{\theta}{360}$ of a whole circle — depends on being able to simplify that fraction quickly and correctly.

from.statement: Rearrange a simple formula to make a different letter the subject, such as rearranging $y=kx$ to find $x$.
from.why_it_matters: Finding a missing radius from a circumference or area, or a missing angle from an arc length, is exactly this kind of rearrangement applied to the circle formulas.

from.statement: Convert between units of length, area and volume (Lesson 5.1).
from.why_it_matters: Some context problems (wheels covering a distance, clock hands sweeping an area) mix units that must be made consistent before substituting into a circle formula.

from.statement: Find the area of a rectangle, triangle, trapezium and circle (Lessons 5.2 and 5.3).
from.why_it_matters: Every prism's volume starts from the area of its cross-section, and a pyramid or cone's total surface area starts from the area of its base — without these area formulas on demand, no solid's volume or surface area can be built.

from.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle.
from.why_it_matters: A cone's slant height, a pyramid's slant height, and the vertical height recovered from a slant height are all found using $l^2=r^2+h^2$ or an equivalent right-angled triangle inside the solid.

from.statement: Convert between units of volume and capacity, such as $\text{cm}^3$ to litres (Lesson 5.1).
from.why_it_matters: Several context problems in this lesson (a tin's capacity, a tank's contents) ask for a final answer in litres or millilitres rather than $\text{cm}^3$.

from.statement: Take the cube root of a number, and recognise cubing as the inverse operation.
from.why_it_matters: Finding a missing radius from a sphere's volume, or a missing side from a cube's volume, both require undoing a cube by taking a cube root.

from.statement: Find the area and perimeter of a rectangle, triangle, trapezium and circle (or a part of one), and the volume and surface area of a prism, cylinder, cone, pyramid and sphere (Lessons 5.2, 5.3 and 5.4).
from.why_it_matters: Every compound shape or solid in this lesson is built by adding or subtracting these exact basic shapes, so each must already be available on demand.

from.statement: Use similar triangles to find a ratio of corresponding lengths.
from.why_it_matters: A frustum's missing cone (the small cone that was sliced off) is recovered by scaling the large cone's dimensions down using a ratio found from similar triangles.

from.statement: Recognise a hemisphere as exactly half a sphere, and a half-cylinder as exactly half a cylinder.
from.why_it_matters: A hemisphere's volume and curved surface area are both exactly half of the corresponding sphere's; forgetting this halving (or halving the wrong quantity) is a common first error when a compound solid includes one.

from.statement: Convert between units of volume and capacity, such as $\text{cm}^3$ to litres (Lesson 5.1).
from.why_it_matters: Several compound-solid context problems (a bucket, a tank) ask for a final answer in litres rather than $\text{cm}^3$.

from.statement: Square a number and find a square root with a calculator, including non-perfect squares.
from.why_it_matters: Every step of Pythagoras' theorem is either squaring a known side or square-rooting a sum of squares; without fluent squaring and rooting, the theorem cannot be applied even when the triangle is set up correctly.

from.statement: Recognise a right angle in a diagram and identify the three vertices and three sides of a triangle.
from.why_it_matters: The whole theorem depends on first finding which angle is the right angle and which side is opposite it; this lesson gives no credit for correct arithmetic applied to the wrong side.

from.statement: Simplify a surd by finding its largest square factor, e.g. $\sqrt{72}=6\sqrt2$.
from.why_it_matters: Several Extended-tier questions ask for an exact length rather than a decimal, and an unsimplified surd such as $\sqrt{72}$ is not accepted as a final 'simplest form' answer.

from.statement: Plot and read coordinates $(x,y)$ on a pair of axes, and find a horizontal or vertical difference between two points.
from.why_it_matters: The distance-between-two-points formula is just Pythagoras' theorem applied to the horizontal and vertical differences; without comfort with coordinates, the formula is a meaningless string of letters.

from.statement: Identify the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle and know that the other two sides are the legs (from Lesson 6.1).
from.why_it_matters: Naming the opposite and adjacent sides is only possible once the hypotenuse is already correctly identified; everything in this lesson is built on that first label.

from.statement: Rearrange a simple equation of the form $\sin\theta=\tfrac{x}{12}$ to make $x$, or $\theta$, the subject.
from.why_it_matters: Every 'find a side' or 'find an angle' question in this lesson reduces to rearranging one short equation; without comfortable algebra here, the correct trigonometric setup still leads to a wrong final answer.

from.statement: Use a scientific calculator to evaluate $\sin$, $\cos$, $\tan$ and their inverse functions in degree mode.
from.why_it_matters: This is a purely mechanical skill, but a calculator left in radian or gradian mode silently produces a wrong answer with no error message, which is the single most common cause of a wrong trigonometry mark in the exam.

from.statement: Understand that bearings are measured clockwise from north and written with three figures (e.g. $065^{\circ}$).
from.why_it_matters: Bearings problems in this lesson assume this convention is already familiar; without it, a correctly drawn triangle can still be converted to the wrong final bearing.

from.statement: Use SOH-CAH-TOA to find a side or an angle in a right-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.2).
from.why_it_matters: Every elevation/depression problem is a right-angled-triangle trigonometry problem in disguise; the new skill in this lesson is entirely about drawing the correct diagram, not about new trigonometric machinery.

from.statement: Recognise alternate angles between a pair of parallel lines cut by a transversal.
from.why_it_matters: The equality 'angle of depression from A to B = angle of elevation from B to A' is proved directly by alternate angles between two parallel horizontal lines; without this, the equality must be memorised rather than understood.

from.statement: Rearrange and solve a linear equation in one unknown, including one with the unknown on both sides.
from.why_it_matters: The two-observer method produces an equation such as $x\tan40^{\circ}=(x+30)\tan25^{\circ}$ with the unknown on both sides; without comfortable algebra here, the correct trigonometric setup cannot be finished.

from.statement: Find the area of a triangle using $\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$.
from.why_it_matters: The 'equal areas' method for the shortest distance from a point to a line, when only the triangle's three sides are known, relies directly on this formula.

from.statement: Use SOH-CAH-TOA to find a side or angle in a right-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.2).
from.why_it_matters: This lesson reuses the exact same ratios; the only change is that the triangle's sides are now expressed as simple numbers and surds instead of a decimal measurement.

from.statement: Simplify a surd and rationalise a denominator of the form $\dfrac{a}{\sqrt b}$.
from.why_it_matters: Every exact-value answer in this lesson is expected in simplified, rationalised form; without this skill a correct trigonometric setup still fails to produce an accepted final answer.

from.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle, including leaving the answer as an exact surd.
from.why_it_matters: Both special triangles in this lesson (the half-square and the half-equilateral triangle) are built by applying Pythagoras' theorem to a triangle with simple whole-number sides.

from.statement: Expand a squared bracket such as $(a+b)^2$ and simplify the result.
from.why_it_matters: Several 'show that' exact-value questions require expanding a bracket containing surds and simplifying term by term; without this algebra skill, the trigonometric substitution alone is not enough to finish the question.

from.statement: Find an acute angle from $\sin,\cos$ or $\tan$ using a calculator's inverse functions (from Lesson 6.2).
from.why_it_matters: The 'first' solution found by a calculator's inverse function is always the starting point from which every other solution on $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$ is generated using symmetry.

from.statement: Recognise the exact trigonometric values and how $\sin,\cos,\tan$ relate to a right-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.4).
from.why_it_matters: The CAST diagram and the graphs extend the SAME three ratios beyond $90^{\circ}$; without a solid right-triangle picture of what $\sin,\cos,\tan$ mean, the extension to a full circle/graph has nothing to build on.

from.statement: Read coordinates and key features (intercepts, turning points, period) from a sketched graph.
from.why_it_matters: The sine, cosine and tangent graphs are read and sketched using exactly this same graph vocabulary.

from.statement: Rearrange a simple linear equation, including one with a negative coefficient (e.g. $6-5c=9\Rightarrow c=-0.6$).
from.why_it_matters: Several equations in this lesson must first be rearranged algebraically into the form $\sin x=k$ or $\tan x=k$ before the graph/CAST method can be applied.

from.statement: Use SOH-CAH-TOA to find a side or angle in a RIGHT-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.2).
from.why_it_matters: The sine and cosine rules are needed precisely because SOH-CAH-TOA only works when there is a right angle; recognising that absence is the trigger for using these new rules.

from.statement: Use the angle sum of a triangle ($180^{\circ}$) to find a missing angle.
from.why_it_matters: The sine rule is frequently combined with the angle sum to find a third angle once two are known, and the ambiguous case specifically requires checking that a candidate angle still leaves $180^{\circ}$ available for the remaining two angles.

from.statement: Rearrange a simple equation to isolate an unknown, including one appearing inside a trigonometric function (e.g. solving $\sin B=0.47$ for $B$).
from.why_it_matters: Every sine/cosine rule calculation ends with an equation of exactly this shape that must be rearranged and then solved with an inverse trigonometric function.

from.statement: Substitute values into a formula and evaluate it correctly, respecting order of operations (from Lesson 6.1, Pythagoras).
from.why_it_matters: The cosine rule and area formula are substitution-heavy; a single misplaced term or order-of-operations slip gives a completely wrong triangle.

from.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.1).
from.why_it_matters: Every 3D calculation in this lesson is built from a SEQUENCE of ordinary 2D Pythagoras calculations; the 3D solid is never solved 'all at once'.

from.statement: Use SOH-CAH-TOA to find an angle in a right-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.2).
from.why_it_matters: Once the correct right-angled triangle has been extracted from the solid, finding the angle inside it is ordinary SOH-CAH-TOA, with no new trigonometric content.

from.statement: Visualise and sketch a simple 3D solid (cuboid, pyramid) from a written description, labelling vertices consistently.
from.why_it_matters: The single hardest part of this lesson is correctly identifying WHICH right-angled triangle inside the solid is relevant; a labelled 3D sketch makes this visible, while working from the description alone invites error.

from.statement: Use the sine rule and cosine rule in a non-right-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.6).
from.why_it_matters: Some pyramid problems extract a triangle (such as a triangular face) that is NOT right-angled, requiring the sine or cosine rule rather than SOH-CAH-TOA.

from.statement: Plot and read the coordinates of a point on a Cartesian grid, including points with negative coordinates.
from.why_it_matters: Every transformation in this lesson is carried out vertex by vertex using coordinates; without being able to plot a point such as $(-2,8)$ confidently, no image can be drawn or checked.

from.statement: Recognise and sketch the horizontal line $y=k$ and the vertical line $x=k$, including the axes $x=0$ and $y=0$.
from.why_it_matters: Every Core mirror line and several rotation centres in this lesson are given exactly this way; confusing $x=k$ (vertical) with $y=k$ (horizontal) makes a reflection answer unreliable from the first line.

from.statement: Count or measure a length directly on a squared grid, and compare two lengths.
from.why_it_matters: Checking that a transformation is congruent (same lengths) or working out an enlarged length both depend on being able to compare lengths read straight off a diagram.

from.statement: Identify the vertices of a simple polygon (triangle, quadrilateral) and label them consistently as corresponding points move.
from.why_it_matters: A transformation is only correct if every corresponding vertex has been tracked without mixing up, for example, which point is $A$ and which is $A'$.

from.statement: Find the coordinates of a translated point, and write a translation as 'image minus object' (from Lesson 7.1).
from.why_it_matters: A column vector $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is found by exactly the same end-minus-start subtraction used for a translation vector; this lesson gives that idea its own notation and extends it to full vector arithmetic.

from.statement: Add, subtract and multiply positive and negative integers and simple fractions confidently and without a calculator.
from.why_it_matters: Every vector calculation in this lesson is two ordinary numerical calculations done in parallel, one per component; a slip with negative numbers corrupts one whole component of the answer.

from.statement: Recognise when two fractions are equivalent, e.g. by cross-multiplying or simplifying.
from.why_it_matters: Checking whether two vectors are parallel is exactly a check that their components are in the same ratio — the same skill as checking two fractions are equivalent.

from.statement: Plot and read coordinates, including negative coordinates, on a Cartesian grid.
from.why_it_matters: Every vector diagram in this lesson is drawn on a coordinate grid, and sketching a vector correctly is the fastest way to sanity-check an algebraic answer.

from.statement: Apply Pythagoras' theorem, $a^2+b^2=c^2$, to find the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle from its two shorter sides.
from.why_it_matters: Every magnitude calculation in this lesson IS a Pythagoras calculation: the vector's two components are the two shorter sides, and the magnitude is the hypotenuse.

from.statement: Write a vector as a column $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}$ and find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ from the coordinates of $A$ and $B$ (from Lesson 7.2).
from.why_it_matters: Finding a distance between two points always starts with finding the connecting vector first; without that step the magnitude formula has nothing to work on.

from.statement: Round a number to $3$ significant figures.
from.why_it_matters: Cambridge IGCSE requires answers to be given exactly or to $3$ significant figures, and almost every magnitude in this lesson involves an irrational square root that must be rounded correctly at the very end.

from.statement: Use a calculator (or recall) to evaluate a square root, and recognise a perfect square.
from.why_it_matters: A magnitude calculation always ends in a square root; recognising that, say, $\sqrt{169}=13$ exactly (rather than reaching for a rounded decimal) keeps 'show that' answers exact where they should be.

from.statement: Add, subtract and find scalar multiples of column vectors, including simplifying an expression such as $\mathbf a+\tfrac12(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)$ (from Lesson 7.2).
from.why_it_matters: Every route in this lesson ends with a vector expression in $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ that must be combined and simplified; without fluent vector algebra the route method cannot be finished.

from.statement: Recognise that two vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other, $\mathbf u=k\mathbf v$ (from Lesson 7.2).
from.why_it_matters: Every parallel or collinear proof in this lesson comes down to spotting that one route vector is a scalar multiple of another.

from.statement: Work confidently with fractions, including adding fractions with different denominators and simplifying a ratio such as $m:n$.
from.why_it_matters: A ratio $AP:PB=m:n$ must be converted to the fraction $\tfrac{m}{m+n}$ of the whole line before it can be used in a vector calculation.

from.statement: Find the midpoint of two coordinates by averaging, $\left(\tfrac{x_1+x_2}{2},\tfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$ (from Lesson 3.4).
from.why_it_matters: The position-vector midpoint formula $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)$ gives exactly the same answer as the coordinate-averaging formula, and checking one against the other is the standard way to catch an error.

from.statement: Simplify a fraction to its lowest terms, and convert confidently between a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
from.why_it_matters: Every probability answer in this lesson must be given as a fraction (simplified), a decimal or a percentage; without fluent conversion, a correctly-counted probability can still be marked wrong for being left in an unsimplified or non-standard form.

from.statement: Count the items in a list or a small set systematically, without missing one or counting one twice (e.g. the letters of a word, the sectors of a spinner).
from.why_it_matters: Every probability calculated by "favourable outcomes over total outcomes" depends entirely on an accurate count of both numbers; a miscount of either one gives a wrong probability even when the method is correct.

from.statement: Read a value from a simple table or bar chart (e.g. the frequency for a given category).
from.why_it_matters: Section 4 of this lesson reads probabilities directly out of frequency tables and bar charts, so being unable to read the chart accurately breaks the probability calculation before it starts.

from.statement: Understand what it means for one collection to overlap with another (the idea behind the words "and", "or" and "neither" applied to two groups).
from.why_it_matters: A Venn diagram sorts the same people or objects into overlapping groups, and misreading what the overlap represents is the single most common source of error when probabilities are read from one.

from.statement: Calculate the theoretical probability of a single event with equally likely outcomes (Lesson 8.1).
from.why_it_matters: Judging whether a die or coin is 'fair' means comparing an experimental relative frequency against the THEORETICAL probability it should match; without the theoretical value from the previous lesson, there is nothing to compare the experiment against.

from.statement: Divide one number by another and express the result as a decimal to an appropriate number of decimal places.
from.why_it_matters: Every relative frequency is a division (frequency ÷ trials), and every expected frequency is a multiplication of a probability by a trial count; both depend on confident, accurate division and multiplication with decimals.

from.statement: Round a number to a sensible degree of accuracy, including to the nearest whole number.
from.why_it_matters: An expected frequency is an average prediction and often comes out as a decimal (e.g. $12.5$); deciding how, or whether, to round it sensibly for a count of real people or objects is a running theme of this lesson.

from.statement: Read and total the frequencies in a simple frequency table.
from.why_it_matters: Every relative-frequency example in this lesson starts from a table of experimental results, and the total of that table is the denominator of every relative frequency calculated from it.

from.statement: Calculate the probability of a single event with equally likely outcomes, and use the complement rule $P(\text{not }A)=1-P(A)$ (Lesson 8.1).
from.why_it_matters: Every sample-space, Venn and tree calculation in this lesson is still, at heart, 'favourable outcomes over total outcomes' or 'multiply/add simple probabilities' — this lesson only changes HOW those outcomes are organised, not the underlying rule.

from.statement: Multiply and add fractions, including fractions with different denominators.
from.why_it_matters: Every tree-diagram answer is a sum of PRODUCTS of fractions (multiply along a branch, add across paths); a slip in fraction arithmetic breaks the final answer even when the probability method is entirely correct.

from.statement: Complete and read a two-set Venn diagram from given totals and an overlap (Lesson 8.1).
from.why_it_matters: This lesson's Venn-diagram work (and the new $P(A\cap B)$, $P(A\cup B)$ notation) is built directly on the 'fill the overlap first' method from Lesson 8.1, now expressed with set notation.

from.statement: List the outcomes of a simple experiment systematically (e.g. the factors of a number, the letters of a word) without missing or repeating one.
from.why_it_matters: A sample space grid is really a systematic list of EVERY pair of outcomes; missing a row, a column or a cell undermines the whole diagram before any probability is read from it.

from.statement: Complete and read a two-set Venn diagram and a simple frequency table, including finding an 'only' region from a circle's total and the overlap (Lessons 8.1 and 8.3).
from.why_it_matters: Every conditional probability in this lesson is read from a DENOMINATOR GROUP inside a table or Venn diagram (a row, a column, a circle); without being able to read that group's total accurately first, there is nothing to divide by.

from.statement: Draw and use a tree diagram with and without replacement, multiplying along branches and adding across paths (Lesson 8.3).
from.why_it_matters: A tree diagram's SECOND-STAGE branches are themselves conditional probabilities, and 'working backwards' on a tree (finding a probability about the first stage from information about the second) is the central new skill of this lesson, built directly on Lesson 8.3's tree method.

from.statement: Divide one fraction by another, and simplify the result.
from.why_it_matters: The general conditional-probability formula $P(A\text{ given }B)=\dfrac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}$ is itself a division of two fractions, and every 'working backwards' tree calculation ends in dividing one path's probability by a sum of several.

from.statement: Use the addition rule $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ and recognise independent events as $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B)$ (Lesson 8.3).
from.why_it_matters: Deciding independence in this lesson means comparing a conditional probability to an ordinary one, which only makes sense once the learner already has a firm, exact notion of what $P(A\cap B)$ and independence mean numerically.

from.statement: Add and subtract whole numbers accurately, including finding a missing total from a sum.
from.why_it_matters: Checking a frequency table (frequencies must sum to the number of data values) and completing a two-way table from row/column totals are both just addition and subtraction done carefully.

from.statement: Read and write inequalities such as $0\le x<10$ on a number line.
from.why_it_matters: Class intervals for continuous data are written as inequalities, and deciding which class a boundary value (e.g. $10$) belongs to depends on reading the inequality signs correctly.

from.statement: Understand the difference between counting (whole-number) quantities and measured quantities.
from.why_it_matters: This is exactly the distinction between discrete and continuous data; without it the whole classification system in this lesson has no foothold.

from.statement: Classify data as categorical, discrete or continuous, and read a simple frequency table (Lesson 9.1).
from.why_it_matters: Every chart in this lesson is just a frequency table redrawn: choosing the right chart, and reading it correctly, both depend on knowing what kind of data and what frequencies it is built from.

from.statement: Simplify a fraction and convert between fractions, decimals and percentages.
from.why_it_matters: Pie-chart angles and the fractions of a total shown by any chart are both simplified the same way, and reading 'what fraction of the total' questions depends on this skill.

from.statement: Measure and draw an angle accurately with a protractor, and recall that angles round a point sum to $360^\circ$.
from.why_it_matters: A pie chart is built entirely from this one fact: splitting $360^\circ$ into sectors proportional to frequency.

from.statement: Add a list of numbers and divide accurately, including with a calculator and by hand.
from.why_it_matters: The mean is nothing more than total divided by count; every error in this lesson that looks conceptual is usually just an arithmetic slip in the total or the count.

from.statement: Order a list of numbers from smallest to largest.
from.why_it_matters: The median, the mode's position and both quartiles are all defined in terms of an ORDERED list; none of them can be found correctly from data as originally given.

from.statement: Read a simple and a grouped frequency table (Lesson 9.1).
from.why_it_matters: Finding an average 'from a frequency table' or 'from grouped data' in this lesson assumes fluent reading of the table structures built in the previous lesson.

from.statement: Calculate the mean, median and range of a data set (Lesson 9.3).
from.why_it_matters: Every comparison in this lesson is built from averages and spreads already calculated exactly as in the previous lesson; this lesson adds the skill of comparing and interpreting them, not of calculating them.

from.statement: Calculate the lower quartile, upper quartile and interquartile range of a data set (Lesson 9.3).
from.why_it_matters: Comparing with the IQR (Extended) requires the IQR to already be calculated correctly; any error here carries straight into a wrong comparison.

from.statement: Read values and totals from a two-way table and a bar chart (Lessons 9.1-9.2).
from.why_it_matters: Interpreting tables and diagrams in this lesson assumes fluent reading of the table and chart structures built in the first two lessons of this unit.

from.statement: Plot coordinates $(x,y)$ accurately on a pair of axes.
from.why_it_matters: Every scatter diagram in this lesson is built from individually plotted coordinate pairs; an inaccurate plot produces a misleading pattern before any statistics is even applied.

from.statement: Calculate the mean of a list of values (Lesson 9.3).
from.why_it_matters: A good line of best fit is checked against the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$, so this lesson assumes the mean can already be calculated fluently for both the $x$-values and the $y$-values.

from.statement: Find the gradient of a line through two given points, and write the equation of a straight line in the form $y=mx+c$.
from.why_it_matters: Finding the equation of a line of best fit from two points on it is ordinary coordinate-geometry gradient work applied to a new context; without it, only the 'by eye' reading skills in this lesson are accessible.

from.statement: Read and build a grouped frequency table, including finding class boundaries and widths (Lesson 9.1).
from.why_it_matters: A cumulative frequency table is built directly from a grouped frequency table by running-totalling its frequencies, so this lesson assumes that structure is already familiar.

from.statement: Define and calculate the median, quartiles and interquartile range of a data set (Lesson 9.3).
from.why_it_matters: This lesson re-uses the exact same definitions (median, $Q_1$, $Q_3$, IQR) but estimates them by reading a curve instead of calculating from a short list, so the underlying concepts must already be secure.

from.statement: Perform linear interpolation between two known values (estimate a value a given fraction of the way between two others).
from.why_it_matters: Reading an estimate between two plotted points on a cumulative frequency curve, whether by eye or by interpolating between table rows, relies on this same 'part-way between two values' reasoning.

from.statement: Read and build a grouped frequency table, including finding class boundaries and widths (Lesson 9.1).
from.why_it_matters: A histogram is built directly from a grouped frequency table; finding each class's width (upper boundary minus lower boundary) correctly is the first and most essential step in finding frequency density.

from.statement: Draw and read an ordinary bar chart with equal class widths (Lesson 9.2).
from.why_it_matters: A histogram looks superficially similar to a bar chart, and this lesson is largely about the specific ways that similarity becomes MISLEADING once class widths are unequal.

from.statement: Estimate the mean of grouped data using class midpoints (Lesson 9.3).
from.why_it_matters: Estimating the mean from a histogram uses exactly the same midpoint-weighted method, applied to frequencies recovered from the histogram's bars rather than read directly from a table.
